title: Copies Everywhere
summary: Quillbook's single database can't keep up with reads, and one dead disk would lose everything. Add followers, then deal with what copies bring: lag, stale reads, failover and two leaders.

goals.text: Scale reads with a leader and followers that replay its log
Explain replication lag and fix stale reads with read-your-writes
Choose between synchronous and asynchronous replication
Walk through a failover and prevent split brain with fencing

steps.title: One database, two problems
body: Quillbook is a shared-notes app. At peak it needs 30,000 reads a second but only 1,500 writes — people open and scroll notes far more than they type.
Everything lives on one database, db-a. It tops out around 10,000 queries a second, and it is the only copy of every note: if its disk dies, so does Quillbook.

card.title: db-a, peak hour
lines: # reads outnumber writes 20 to 1

steps.title: A leader and two followers
body: Replication keeps full copies of the data on several machines. One is the leader: all writes go there. It records each change in its log — the same write-ahead log it already keeps for crash safety.

Followers stream that log and replay it in the same order, so they converge on the same data. The API sends reads to the followers: three nodes now share the read load, and losing one disk no longer loses the notes.
changes: + db-b and db-c follow db-a's log
~ Reads go to followers, writes to the leader

card.title: Replication = ship the log
lines: 1. every write goes to the leader
2. the leader appends it to its log
3. followers stream the log and replay it in order
= any copy can answer reads

steps.title: Followers live slightly in the past
body: By default the leader confirms a write before followers have it — asynchronous replication. Usually they're a fraction of a second behind. During a bulk import, db-c falls 6 seconds behind: that's replication lag.
Mia saves a note and reloads. Her save went to the leader; the reload is served by db-c, which hasn't replayed it yet. Her edit appears to have vanished.

callout.text: Lag is normally invisible, then spikes exactly when the system is busiest. Monitor it and alert on it.

changes: + Mia saves, then reloads from db-c

card.title: Mia's 2 seconds
lines: 09:00:00  save note → leader ✓
09:00:01  reload → db-c
! db-c is still replaying 08:59:55
! Mia sees her old text

steps.title: Read-your-writes
body: Most readers don't mind a note being a few seconds old. The author does. Read-your-writes consistency guarantees that you always see your own changes.

A simple way: for a short window after someone writes, send their reads to the leader. A more precise way: remember the log position of their last write and only read from a follower that has replayed past it. Everyone else keeps hitting the followers.
changes: ~ Mia's reads go to the leader for ~10 s after she writes

card.title: Read-your-writes
lines: after a write, remember its log position
send that user's reads to a copy that has it —
or to the leader for the next ~10 s
= everyone else keeps using followers

steps.title: Synchronous vs asynchronous
body: If the leader dies, writes it confirmed but hadn't shipped yet are gone. Synchronous replication closes that gap: the leader waits for a follower to confirm before telling the client “OK”.
The price is latency on every write, and availability: if the sync follower stalls, writes stall too. A common middle ground is semi-synchronous — one follower in sync (db-b), the rest async.

callout.text: Making every follower synchronous means the slowest one sets your write latency — and any one failing blocks all writes.

card.title: Who must confirm a write?
lines: async: leader says OK at once
! a crash can lose the last moments of writes
sync: leader waits for a follower's ack
= acked writes exist on two machines
# semi-sync: one sync follower, the rest async

steps.title: The leader dies
body: At 03:12 db-a stops responding. Reads carry on — the followers have the data — but every write fails, because only the leader may accept writes.
Someone (or something) has to decide that db-a is really gone and not just slow, and pick a replacement.

steps.title: Promote a follower
body: Failover: after missing heartbeats for a timeout (here 10 s), the cluster promotes the most up-to-date follower. db-b was synchronous, so it has every confirmed write.

The API and db-c are pointed at the new leader. Writes resume after about 30 seconds. The timeout is a trade-off: too short and a slow network triggers needless failovers; too long and writes stay down.

card.title: Failover in 3 moves
lines: 1. detect: no heartbeat from db-a for 10 s
2. promote the most up-to-date follower (db-b)
3. point the API and db-c at the new leader
= writes back after ~30 s

steps.title: Split brain
body: db-a wasn't dead — a network switch had cut it off. It comes back still believing it's the leader, and one API node with stale config keeps sending it writes.
Now two machines accept writes for the same notes and their histories diverge: split brain. Merging them afterwards is painful, and some edits will be lost either way.

callout.text: Failover is the riskiest moment in a replicated system. Most data-loss stories start with two nodes both thinking they lead.

changes: ~ db-a back, still acting as leader
+ Stale API path writes to db-a

card.title: Two leaders
lines: db-a was only cut off — now it's back
! it still accepts writes from a stale API node
! db-a and db-b now hold different histories
# async writes db-a never shipped are also lost

steps.title: Fence off the old leader
body: Every promotion bumps a term (or epoch) number: db-b leads term 8, db-a led term 7. Writes and replication messages carry the term, and nodes reject anything from an older term.
So db-a's writes bounce, it learns a newer leader exists, discards what it never replicated and rejoins as a follower of db-b.

card.title: Fencing with a term number
lines: each promotion bumps the term: 7 → 8
every write carries the term it was sent under
= replicas reject writes from an older term
old leader steps down and follows db-b

steps.title: Copies are cheap; keeping them honest isn't
body:
• A leader takes writes; followers replay its log and serve reads.
  • Async replication is fast but followers lag; sync guarantees acked writes survive, at a latency cost.
  • Use read-your-writes routing so users always see their own changes.
  • Failover promotes a follower; fencing with term numbers stops the old leader from causing split brain.

card.title: Replication checklist
lines: followers add read capacity and spare copies
async is fast but lags; sync is safe but slower
route a user's reads after their writes
rehearse failover; fence the old leader
